## Calendar description

> *3.5 (fi) (either term, 3-1S-0). Formulation and solution of materials engineering problems; solution of systems of linear and nonlinear algebraic equations; materials modeling and simulation techniques that cover different time and length scales, which include density functional theory methods, Monte Carlo, molecular dynamics, phase field, finite element method, and machine learning approaches; hands-on experience with several modern materials modeling codes.*

## Prerequisites

ENCMP 100 (or equivalent), MATH 102, MATH 201, and MATH 209, subject to confirmation against the current University Calendar.

## Course purpose

MATE 374 develops the numerical judgement needed to turn a materials question into a trustworthy computational result. Students will formulate mathematical problems, select and apply numerical methods, examine the effects of approximation and finite precision, and interpret calculations at several materials length and time scales.

Python is the main language used for small transparent calculations. Established scientific libraries and materials-simulation software are introduced where they help answer an engineering question. Programming mechanics remain subordinate to model choice, error analysis, verification, and physical interpretation.

## Course learning outcomes

By the end of the course, given a materials problem, dataset, or computational result, students should be able to:

1. **Formulate** the physical question as a mathematical problem with stated variables, assumptions, scales, units, and conditions.
2. **Select** a suitable numerical method by considering the mathematical structure, required accuracy, robustness, and computational cost.
3. **Implement or inspect** core numerical procedures for scalar equations, optimization, data analysis, coupled systems, and evolution problems.
4. **Distinguish and diagnose** model-form, input, sampling, discretization, iterative, implementation, and floating-point sources of error or uncertainty.
5. **Verify** a computation using appropriate evidence such as residuals, refinement, limiting cases, conservation, units, or comparison with a reference result.
6. **Interpret** a result as a materials-engineering conclusion while stating the model's domain and limitations.
7. **Document and reproduce** a computational study using clear code, recorded inputs, software information, and an honest account of tool use.
8. **Relate** continuum, mesoscale, atomistic, and electronic simulation approaches to the questions and mathematical forms they are designed to address.

## Course organization

The course is organized into distinct units, themed around questions:

| Unit | Organizing question | Main ideas |
|---|---|---|
| Orientation and numerical thinking | Can I trust this calculation? | approximation, convergence, floating point, performance |
| Finding special points | Where is a root, equilibrium, or minimum? | bisection, fixed point, secant, Newton, optimization |
| Functions and data | What can sampled values support? | differentiation, integration, interpolation, regression |
| Coupled systems | How do several variables interact? | vectors, matrices, linear and nonlinear systems |
| Evolution in time | How does a material state change? | ODE formulation, timestep error, stability, established solvers |
| Fields and conservation | How does change move through a material? | fluxes, grids, boundary conditions, PDE discretization |
| Simulation across scales | Which representation fits the question? | phase field, Monte Carlo, MD, electronic structure, modern data-driven links |

## Learning materials and computing

The [course notes](../units/index.qmd) are the main reference and are designed for both browser reading and printing. Interactive activities use marimo notebooks in the browser where practical. Molab (hosted marimo notebooks by `https://molab.marimo.io`) or local Unix workstations may be used for completing the heavier computational loads and / or using simulation packages.

Use a modern web browser, such as Chrome, Firefox, or Safari, to read the course notes and run the interactive Python notebooks. Browser-based activities let you edit code, run it, and view the results without installing Python. You may also download the source code and run it locally; this is optional, but useful if you want to experiment beyond the activities.

### Recommended references

The course does not require an official textbook, as the course materials contain the cannonical sources, code examples and interactive demos within itself. However, students are strongly recommended to check the following alternative sources

**Numerical methods and implementations**

- J. Kiusalaas, [*Numerical Methods in Engineering with Python 3*](https://ualberta.primo.exlibrisgroup.com/view/action/uresolver.do?operation=resolveService&package_service_id=19059219040009116&institutionId=9116&customerId=9115&VE=true).
- E. Sullivan, [*Numerical Methods: An Inquiry-Based Approach with Python*](https://numericalmethodssullivan.github.io/index.html).

**Computational methods and analysis**

- J. Mmbaga, R. Hayes, K. Nandakumar, and M. Flynn, *Computational Methods for Engineers: Modeling, Algorithms and Analysis*. (Available at UofA library as hard copy)

**Concepts in materials science and engineering**

- W. D. Callister Jr. and D. G. Rethwisch, *Materials Science and Engineering: An Introduction*. (Available at UofA library as hard copy)

## Assessment

| Assessment | Weight | Working form |
|---|---:|---|
| Assignments | 20% | **Five (5)** computational investigations; **best four (4)** counted |
| Group project | 20% | Materials simulation study and final report |
| Midterm examination | 20% | 50-minute in-class examination; tentative week of October 28 |
| Final examination | 40% | Two-hour examination scheduled by the University |
| **Total** | **100%** | |

### Notes on assessment

Each assignment will normally be available for approximately two weeks. An assignment may ask you to:

1. complete a step-by-step derivation or calculation by hand;
2. write or edit Python code to implement a numerical method and solve a particular problem; or
3. use interactive controls to manipulate a program and report your findings.

### Assignment timing and late work

Five assignments will be released through Canvas, each with approximately two weeks for completion. The four highest assignment grades will count toward the assignment component.

A late submission will lose 25% of the assignment mark for each 24-hour period after the deadline. If illness or an emergency delays your work, contact the instructor and TA as soon as possible. The circumstances and any requested adjustment will be reviewed case by case.

### Project

You will work in groups of approximately five on a realistic multiscale materials-simulation problem. Where practical, you will interact with the problem through a Python-based interface. Your group will construct and submit a final report that clearly presents:

- the problem identification and motivation;
- the key theoretical background;
- the simulation details, including the model, assumptions, parameters, numerical methods, and implementation; and
- the results and their materials-engineering interpretation.

## Examinations and permitted resources

Both the midterm and final examinations will be open-book examinations. You may use a laptop or tablet to access the course website, course notes, Python notebooks, and official Python/API documentation. Exam questions may require you to complete, run, interpret, or diagnose short Python programs within the time limit.

Generative-AI tools and communication with other people are not permitted during examinations. Any additional device or proctoring instructions will be provided before each examination.

**No formula sheet** will be provided. Because the examinations are open book, you are encouraged to prepare concise notes on the methods and concepts covered in the course.

- A survey about midterm availability will be sent in late September to identify scheduling conflicts.

- The University has not yet released the final examination schedule. This syllabus will be updated once the schedule is available.

## Academic integrity and AI-assisted work

Students are responsible for following the University of Alberta Student Academic Integrity Policy and for understanding the permitted collaboration stated on each assessment.

AI-assisted coding is **permitted** for assignments and the project unless a task explicitly states otherwise. Students remain responsible for the correctness and authorship of submitted work. They must be able to explain the model, algorithm, code, verification, and interpretation.

Any submitted work that used an AI-assisted tool must include a **short disclosure** naming the tool and describing its contribution. Students must not submit generated code or prose they cannot defend, fabricate results or citations, or enter confidential, personal, proprietary, or restricted data into external services.

A course-specific [Gemini assistant](https://gemini.google.com/gem/7d47e82eecb2) is available as an optional coding aid. University guidance and the assessment-specific rules still apply.

## Accommodations, illness, and missed work

If you require accommodations, register through the University's approved process and contact the instructor and TA as early as possible, preferably at least two weeks before an accommodated examination. This gives us time to confirm that the course materials, software, and examination environment are accessible in the approved setting.

Per University of Alberta regulations, there will be **no deferred
midterm examination**. If illness or an emergency affects your ability
to write the midterm, contact the instructor and TA as soon as possible
**before the examination**. Any adjustment to the assessment weighting
will be reviewed case by case and will follow University
policy. Deferred final examinations and other missed term work will
follow the applicable Faculty and University procedures.



## Respectful learning environment and recordings

Treat your classmates, instructor, teaching assistant, and other members of the University community with respect. Questions, disagreement, and constructive criticism are welcome; harassment, discrimination, intimidation, and disruptive conduct are not.

Course materials, class recordings, and student work may not be copied, recorded, or redistributed except as permitted by the University, the copyright holder, or an approved accommodation. Recordings, when provided, are for use by enrolled students in this course.
